question: Aristotle's law of motion held that:
options: An external force is required to keep a body in motion
Friction is needed for all motion
Rest and uniform motion are equivalent
explanation: Aristotle held an external force is needed to keep a body moving — wrong, it is only needed to counter friction (Sec. 4.2).

question: Galileo concluded from the double inclined-plane experiment that a ball released from rest on a frictionless horizontal plane would:
explanation: With the second plane horizontal and friction absent, the ball's motion never ceases — the state of uniform motion needs no force (Sec. 4.3).

question: Newton's first law states that if the net external force on a body is zero, then:
options: Its speed must be constant but direction can change
explanation: The first law: zero net external force implies zero acceleration — the body is at rest or in uniform linear motion.

question: Momentum of a body is best defined as:
options: The product of its mass and velocity
The total external force on it
Its kinetic energy divided by time
The product of force and time
explanation: p = mv (Eq. 4.1). The product of force and time is impulse.

question: The SI unit of force, the newton, is:
explanation: With k = 1, F = ma; one newton gives 1 kg a 1 m s⁻² acceleration: 1 N = 1 kg m s⁻².

question: The second law of motion is a VECTOR law. This means:
options: F = ma holds component-wise (Fₓ = maₓ, etc.)
Only the horizontal component of velocity can change
explanation: F = dp/dt is equivalent to three scalar equations, one per direction. A force changes only the velocity component parallel to itself (Eq. 4.6).

question: A bullet of mass 0.04 kg travelling at 90 m s⁻¹ is stopped in 60 cm. The average retarding force on it is:
explanation: a = −u²/2s = −8100/1.2 = −6750 m s⁻²; F = 0.04 × 6750 = 270 N (Example 4.2). This is only the average value.

question: A batsman hits a 0.15 kg ball (12 m s⁻¹) straight back at the same speed. The impulse imparted to the ball is:
explanation: Δp = 0.15×12 − (−0.15×12) = 3.6 N s toward the bowler (Example 4.4).

question: Two identical billiard balls reflect off a wall — one normally, one at 30° to the normal. The force on the wall due to each ball is:
options: Normal to the wall in both cases
Inclined at 30° to the normal in case (b)
Along the incoming velocity in each case
explanation: Momentum parallel to the wall is unchanged in every collision; the impulse (hence force) is always normal to the wall (Example 4.5).

question: The ratio of the impulse magnitudes in Example 4.5 (normal hit : 30° hit) is:
explanation: Ratio = 2mu/(2mu cos30°) = 1/cos30° = 2/√3 ≈ 1.2 (Example 4.5).

question: Which statement about the third law is TRUE?
options: Action and reaction act on the same body and cancel
Action and reaction are simultaneous mutual forces on different bodies
Reaction is always smaller than action
explanation: There is no cause–effect relation; the forces act at the same instant on DIFFERENT bodies, so they can never be added for a single body (Sec. 4.6).

question: A 6 kg mass hangs from a rope; a 50 N horizontal force pulls the rope's mid-point. In equilibrium the rope makes with the vertical an angle θ such that:
explanation: T₁cosθ = 60 N and T₁sinθ = 50 N → tanθ = 50/60 = 5/6, θ ≈ 40° (Example 4.6).

question: A box stays put on the floor of an accelerating train. What provides the box's acceleration?
options: Static friction between box and floor
There is no acceleration of the box
explanation: The only horizontal force conceivable on the box is static friction, which provides the same acceleration as the train (Sec. 4.9.1).

question: A block just begins to slide on a plane inclined at 15°. The coefficient of static friction is:
explanation: μₛ = tan θₘₐₓ = tan 15° ≈ 0.27 — independent of the block's mass (Example 4.8).

question: For the 3 kg block + 20 kg trolley system (μₖ = 0.04, g = 10 m s⁻²), the acceleration and tension are:
The maximum speed of a car on a LEVEL circular road of radius R is:
explanation: Static friction alone supplies mv²/R ≤ μₛN = μₛmg → vₘₐₓ = √(μₛRg), independent of mass (Eq. 4.18).

question: A cyclist at 18 km/h takes a level turn of radius 3 m with μₛ = 0.1 (g = 9.8 m s⁻²). The cyclist:
options: Does not slip — friction is ample
explanation: v = 5 m s⁻¹, v² = 25; the available μₛRg = 0.1×3×9.8 = 2.94 m²s⁻² — condition v² ≤ μₛRg fails, so he slips (Example 4.10).

question: On a road banked at θ with coefficient μₛ, driving at the optimum speed v₀ = (Rg tanθ)^½:
options: Requires maximum friction up the slope
Needs NO friction to provide centripetal force
explanation: At v₀ the horizontal component of N alone supplies the centripetal force; friction is not needed — hence minimal tyre wear. For v < v₀ friction acts up the slope (Sec. 4.10).

question: The motion of a particle of mass m is y = ut + ½gt². Show the force is mg.
answer: v = dy/dt = u + gt, so a = dv/dt = g. Hence F = ma = mg — the particle moves under gravity, y measured down.
explanation: Example 4.3: differentiate twice, apply F = ma.

question: A nucleus at rest disintegrates into two fragments. Why must the fragments move in opposite directions?
answer: Initially the system momentum is zero. In the absence of external forces momentum is conserved, so p₁ + p₂ = 0 — the two fragments carry equal and opposite momenta along the same line.
explanation: Exercise 4.17: conservation of momentum.

question: A 70 kg man rides a lift. Find the scale reading (i) going up at constant 10 m s⁻¹, (ii) accelerating down at 5 m s⁻², (iii) falling freely.
answer: (i) R = mg = 700 N. (ii) R = m(g − a) = 70 × 5 = 350 N. (iii) Free fall: R = 0 N — weightlessness.
explanation: Exercise 4.13: scale reads the normal force, not the weight. mg = R only in equilibrium.

question: A three-wheeler of total mass 465 kg is brought to rest from 36 km/h in 4.0 s. What average retarding force is applied?
explanation: Exercise 4.8: Newton's second law with the total mass (vehicle + driver).

question: A 0.40 kg body moving north at 10 m s⁻¹ is subject to a constant 8.0 N force south for 30 s. Find its position at t = 100 s.
explanation: Exercise 4.10: uniform acceleration; quadratic position.

question: A stone of mass 0.25 kg on a 1.5 m string whirls at 40 rev/min. Find the tension, and the maximum speed if the string can take 200 N.
answer: ω = 2π×40/60 ≈ 4.19 rad s⁻¹. T = mω²r = 0.25 × 17.55 × 1.5 ≈ 6.6 N. vₘₐₓ = √(Tr/m) = √(200 × 1.5/0.25) ≈ 34.6 m s⁻¹. If exceeded, the stone flies off tangentially.
explanation: Exercise 4.21: centripetal force = tension.
